title: The rock that was once on fire
teaches: How molten rock cools into glass or crystals, and how a lava flow cracks into columns

blocks.text: In 1751 the French naturalist Jean-Étienne Guettard was travelling through Moulins, in central France, when the roadside milestones caught his eye. They were cut from a dark, porous stone that resembled a rigid sponge. Guettard knew of stone like it from the slopes of Vesuvius in Italy: **lava**, molten rock that has poured from a volcano and solidified, its gas bubbles frozen in place.

When he asked where the stone was quarried, he was directed to Volvic, in the Auvergne hills near Clermont-Ferrand. Above the quarries stood a line of rounded hills, several of them hollowed at the summit like bowls. They were extinct volcanoes, dozens of them, now known as the Chaîne des Puys, though no historical record mentioned their ever having erupted.

blocks.caption: The Chaîne des Puys, a chain of roughly eighty small volcanoes west of Clermont-Ferrand. The rounded hills are cones, many with summit craters.

options.title: The volcanoes of Auvergne
options.alt: A shaded relief map of a line of round volcanic hills running north to south, with Puy de Dôme, Puy de Pariou, Volvic and Clermont-Ferrand marked.

blocks.caption: Puy de Pariou, a cinder cone with a summit crater.

blocks.text: Finding dead volcanoes in the middle of France was a surprise, though one that threatened nobody's grand theories. The real dispute centred on a different, far more abundant rock called **basalt**, and whether it had once been molten like lava or had precipitated from water like the sedimentary strata of Lesson 1.

blocks.title: Hold on to
points: In 1751, Guettard traced a porous dark building stone in central France back to an unrecorded chain of extinct volcanoes.
Lava is molten rock that has erupted at the surface and solidified.

blocks.text: Basalt is the most common volcanic rock on Earth, forming the bulk of the oceanic crust. Freshly broken, it is black or dark grey, dense, hard, and **fine-grained**, meaning its component crystals are too small to distinguish without a lens. In places it fractures into tall, flat-sided columns packed together like pencils in a box; the Giant's Causeway in Northern Ireland exposes tens of thousands of them.

blocks.caption: The Giant's Causeway, Northern Ireland. Most of the columns have five, six, or seven sides.

blocks.text: The most influential geology teacher of the late eighteenth century, Abraham Gottlob Werner at the Freiberg Mining Academy in Saxony, held that nearly all rocks, basalt included, had precipitated out of a primordial ocean that once covered the globe, much as salt crystallises from brine. His followers became known as **Neptunists**, after the Roman sea god. Because crystals naturally grow with flat faces and regular geometry, the Neptunists mistook the neat columns of basalt for giant crystals settled from water. Lava, in their view, was an altogether different material, rough and vesicular, restricted to local coal fires and active volcanoes.

In 1763 another Frenchman, Nicolas Desmarest, walked the Auvergne. He found basalt columns there as well, and traced the rock units containing them uphill. They ran in long tongues down from the volcanic cones and along the valley floors, following the topography just as liquid lava does. The upper surfaces of these tongues were rough and riddled with gas cavities, identical to fresh lava, while lower down within the very same sheets the rock was dense and divided into columns. A rock that pours from a cone, flows down valleys, and froths at its top is lava. Basalt, Desmarest concluded, was simply chilled lava.

The columns themselves are the product of thermal contraction. A thick lava flow loses heat from its upper surface into the air and from its base into the cold ground below. As the solidifying rock cools, it shrinks and pulls itself apart, much like mud cracking in the sun. Fractures initiate at the chilled surfaces in an irregular network and propagate inward as the cooling front advances into the interior of the flow.

blocks.caption: Cracks in a cooling lava flow viewed in horizontal section at successive depths. Six-sided columns are shaded blue-grey.
blocks.task: Increase the depth into the flow until most of the polygons have settled into hexagons

blocks.text: As the fracture network advances inward, each crack follows the path established above it but migrates slightly toward meeting its neighbours at 120-degree junctions, the geometry that relieves tension most efficiently. A few tens of centimetres beneath the surface, the initial jumble organises itself predominantly into hexagons, mingled with pentagons and heptagons so that the average number of sides remains close to six. Where lava cools rapidly, thermal stress accumulates faster and fractures nucleate closer together, producing narrower columns.

blocks.caption: The glacially planed tops of basalt columns at Devils Postpile, California, showing the polygonal network in cross-section.

blocks.title: Hold on to
points: Neptunists argued that basalt precipitated from a primordial ocean, mistaking its polygonal columns for giant crystals.
Desmarest demonstrated that basalt is volcanic by mapping columnar basalt sheets continuously back to cinder cones in Auvergne.
Columnar jointing forms as cooling lava contracts and fractures inward from its surfaces, self-organising into a mostly hexagonal network.

blocks.text: Desmarest's argument rested on field mapping, but the Neptunists had a laboratory objection. Whenever rock from Vesuvius or Etna was remelted in a crucible and allowed to cool, it solidified into a shiny black glass. Natural basalt, however, has a dull, stony texture composed of microscopic crystals. If basalt had truly cooled from a melt, the Neptunists asked, why was it stony rather than glassy?

In Edinburgh, Sir James Hall resolved to test the question experimentally. Hall was a close friend of James Hutton, who had argued that subterranean heat was the primary agent in rock formation. In the late 1790s, after Hutton's death, Hall took samples of Scottish basalt and dolerite, melted them in a reverberatory glasshouse furnace, and varied the rate at which the crucible cooled.

blocks.caption: Simulated cooling of a silicate melt. Above, a 2 cm field of view; below, the resulting rock type.
blocks.task: Make a prediction, then adjust the cooling time until the basalt melt grows visible crystals

blocks.text: Quenched over a minute or two, the melt solidified into black glass, indistinguishable from the chilled rind of a fresh lava flow. Allowed to cool slowly over hours, however, the identical melt crystallised into a dull, stony mass closely resembling the original rock. Cooling rate alone determined whether the melt became glass or stone. A crystal is a solid whose atoms are arranged in a periodic, three-dimensional lattice, and a **mineral** is a naturally occurring crystalline compound with a specific chemical composition, such as quartz or feldspar. In a liquid melt, atoms move freely; given sufficient time as the temperature drops, they diffuse into their lowest-energy lattice positions. Cooled too quickly, they are arrested in disorder, forming an amorphous solid: a **glass**.

The slower the cooling, the fewer and larger the crystals that grow. Lava cooling at the surface over days to years yields fine-grained basalt. The same magma cooling underground over decades or centuries forms **dolerite** (called diabase in North America), whose interlocking crystals measure around a millimetre; insulated deep in the crust over tens of thousands of years, it grows crystals several millimetres across, easily seen with the unaided eye, forming **gabbro**.

blocks.title: Hold on to
points: James Hall showed that melted basalt quenches to glass when cooled rapidly, but recrystallises into a stony texture when cooled slowly.
Crystal size in an igneous rock is governed by cooling rate: rapid cooling yields glass or microscopic grains, while slow underground cooling grows coarse crystals.

blocks.text: Rocks that solidify from a molten state are termed **igneous**, from the Latin *ignis* (fire). They are classified along two axes: cooling history, which governs grain size, and chemical composition of the melt, which determines the mineral assemblage and colour.

Melts rich in iron and magnesium crystallise into dark minerals, producing basalt when chilled rapidly at the surface and gabbro when cooled slowly at depth. Melts rich in **silica** (silicon dioxide, the primary constituent of quartz and common window glass) crystallise into pale minerals: rhyolite at the surface, **granite** deep underground, or obsidian if chilled so abruptly that no crystals form at all. When a viscous, gas-charged silica melt depressurises during an eruption, exsolving gas froths the liquid into **pumice**, a glassy foam porous enough to float on water.

blocks.caption: Granite, cooled slowly at depth over thousands of years. The visible grains are grey glassy quartz, pink and white feldspar, and dark biotite mica.

blocks.text: In 1785 Hutton had travelled to Glen Tilt in the Scottish Highlands to test his conviction that coarse-grained granite had also once been molten. In the bed of the River Tilt he found veins of pink granite branching upward into the overlying layered schists and limestones, having clearly been injected into fractures as a liquid. By the principle of cross-cutting relationships from Lesson 1, the granite had to be younger than the strata it penetrated, refuting Werner's claim that granite was the oldest rock on Earth, precipitated first onto the floor of the primordial ocean. Field evidence of this kind, paired with Hall's furnace experiments, gradually dismantled Neptunism; by the 1820s, the igneous origin of both basalt and granite was broadly accepted.

blocks.caption: From roadside milestones to the foundry furnace: establishing the igneous origin of basalt and granite.

events.label: Guettard traces the Moulins milestones to volcanoes in Auvergne
Desmarest maps columnar basalt back to lava flows
Hutton observes intrusive granite veins in Glen Tilt
Werner publishes his Neptunist classification of basalt
Hall melts basalt and recrystallises it by slow cooling
Geologists broadly accept that basalt and granite were molten

blocks.title: Hold on to
points: Igneous rocks solidify from molten rock (magma underground, lava at the surface).
Grain size records cooling rate: glass and fine-grained rocks cool quickly at or near the surface; coarse-grained rocks cool slowly at depth.
Composition controls mineralogy and colour: iron- and magnesium-rich melts yield dark rocks (basalt, gabbro), whereas silica-rich melts yield pale rocks (rhyolite, granite).

blocks.caption: Six questions on igneous rocks and cooling history
blocks.task: Select the best answer for each question

items.ask: This specimen is entirely glassy, with no crystals visible even under a lens. What does this texture indicate about its cooling history?
choices: It chilled too rapidly for diffusing atoms to organise into crystal lattices
It cooled steadily over several weeks at the base of a thick flow
It solidified slowly beneath a thick blanket of overlying rock
items.why: Glass forms when a melt quenches so quickly that its atoms are frozen in place before they can arrange into orderly mineral lattices. This silica-rich glass is obsidian.

items.ask: The individual mineral grains in this rock are several millimetres across. In what environment did the melt most likely solidify?
choices: Deep in the crust, insulated by surrounding rock over thousands of years
At the surface, pouring out as a thin lava sheet
Near the chilled upper margin of a lava lake
items.why: Growing crystals several millimetres across requires sustained heat and slow cooling over thousands of years, conditions found deep underground. This rock is granite.

items.ask: Neptunists argued that basalt could not be volcanic because remelted lava cooled into glass in laboratory crucibles, whereas basalt is stony. How did James Hall refute this?
choices: He showed that melted basalt returns to a stony, crystalline state if cooled slowly enough
He demonstrated that basaltic glass devitrifies only when submerged in seawater
He proved that natural basalt melts at a higher temperature than foundry furnaces could reach
items.why: By controlling the cooling rate of his furnace, Hall showed that the same basaltic melt produces black glass when quenched and a stony, crystalline rock when cooled over hours.

items.ask: What field evidence convinced Nicolas Desmarest that the basalt columns of Auvergne were solidified lava?
choices: The columnar sheets were continuous with vesicular tongues of rock extending down from volcanic cones
The basalt columns remained noticeably warm from residual volcanic heat
The six-sided columns matched the crystal habit of minerals found around active fumaroles
items.why: Desmarest mapped the columnar basalt continuously uphill into scoriaceous, bubbly sheets that issued directly from the craters of the Auvergne cones.

items.ask: Two basaltic lava flows exhibit columnar jointing. Flow A has columns 20 cm in diameter; Flow B has columns 2 metres in diameter. Which flow cooled more rapidly?
choices: Flow A, with the 20 cm columns
Flow B, with the 2 metre columns
Neither; column diameter is governed by melt composition rather than cooling rate
items.why: Faster cooling builds thermal stress more rapidly, causing fractures to nucleate closer together and dividing the rock into narrower columns.

items.ask: Why is pumice buoyant enough to float on water?
choices: Escaping volcanic gases inflated the viscous melt into a frothy glass full of sealed vesicles
It crystallises exclusively from low-density lithium and beryllium minerals
Hydrocarbons trapped during eruption coat the pores and repel water
items.why: When gas-rich silica magma decompresses upon eruption, exsolving bubbles turn the melt into a foam that freezes as glass before the gas can escape, giving the rock a bulk density lower than water.

learned: Desmarest settled the field origin of basalt by mapping columnar sheets in Auvergne continuously back to volcanic cones.
James Hall proved experimentally that a silicate melt quenches to glass when chilled rapidly, but grows interlocking crystals when cooled slowly.
Columnar jointing develops as a cooling lava flow contracts, propagating fractures inward that self-organise into a predominantly hexagonal network.
Igneous rocks are classified by grain size (recording cooling rate) and mineral composition (reflecting whether the melt was rich in iron and magnesium or in silica).
